CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION INVOLVED
The Preamble to the Bill of Rights states, in
relevant part:
The Conventions of a number of the
States, having at the time of their
adopting the Constitution, expressed a
desire, in order to prevent
misconstruction or abuse of its powers,
that further declaratory and restrictive
clauses should be added: And as
extending the ground of public
confidence in the Government, will best
ensure the beneficent ends of its
institution.
The Second Amendment provides:
A well regulated Militia, being
necessary to the security of a free State,
the right of the people to keep and bear
Arms, shall not be infringed.

INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
Amicus, American Enlightenment Project, a
District of Columbia non-profit, was founded on the
tenth anniversary of District of Columbia v. Heller to
address the post-Heller epidemic of gun violence. The
Project seeks to show that Heller was wrongly
decided, that the Second Amendment protects no
individual right, and that its full text remains
unconstrued.

Amicus is represented by counsel experienced in
resolving unsettled legal questions. Counsel’s
resolution of a half-century conflict over high-seas air
crashes was unanimou sly adopted in Zicherman v.
Korean Air Lines, 516 U.S. 217 (1996) (Scalia, J.). In
October 2015, counsel’s brief led justices to conclude
that “substantial contact,” undecided for decades,
simply means “minimum contacts.” See Foreign
Sovereign Immunities Act: ‘Bedlam’ Redux  (Law360,
Sept. 22, 2017). Months later, counsel published 2nd
Amendment Still Undecided (Law360, Jan. 11, 2016),
followed by related articles, including Court Pauses
Joyriding with AR-15s (Nat’l L. Rev., July 21, 2025),
addressing issues presented here. 2

INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF
ARUGMENT

A disciplined citizens’ militia,
being necessary to the ____ of a free polity,
the right of citizens to possess and carry
weapons commonly used for self-defense,
shall not be ______.
— District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570,
592, 597, 600, 625 (2008)

This brief addresses the question Justice Barrett
posed at argument in Bruen: whether Heller “was
rightly decided.” N.Y.S. Rifle & Pistol Ass'n v. Bruen,
597 U.S. 1 (2022); Tr. 89 (Nov. 3, 2021). The Court
should now confront that question. At minimum,
Heller has no binding effect in these AR-15-ban cases.

Heller did not address the Amendment’s legal
context, its actual antecedents, purpose, origins, or
full text. It did not construe “security”; the “free
State” secured; the “right of the people” as a public
right; or “shall not be infringed,” the constitutional
command. It construed “keep and bear Arms” under
the wrong body of law. And it never construed the
Amendment as a whole. A decision that did not decide
those issues cannot control them now.

Through remarkable failures of the adversary
system, the Court was only asked to choose between
historical fictions—individual rights tied to militia
service or to self-d efense—that were undebated at
founding, difficult to reconcile with James Madison’s
conscientious-objector clause, and drew “interpretive
blood from so few evidentiary turnips.” Br. of Amici

 
Curiae Jack Rakove, et al. 4, No. 07-290. An amicus
in support of neither party in Bruen warned:
“Historical claims based on conjecture” are “nothing
more than historical fiction” and should not receive
“the imprimatur of this Court.” Br. of Amicus Patrick
Charles 20, No. 20-843. Resolving that false choice,
the Court never addressed the Amendment’s actual
text or meaning.

A similar error was avoided last Term. A single
amicus showed that “regular forces” in a militia
statute referred to military forces—not law
enforcement, as both sides argued. The Court ordered
rebriefing in Trump v. Illinois , No. 25A443 (Dec. 23,
2025), correcting course before precedent could
distort military authority. The same course
correction is warranted here.

Like that militia statute, the Amendment arose
from the Anglo-American militia system: the law
organizing citizen-soldiers and prescribing arms,
readiness, muster, service, and discipline. It did not
arise from the separate body of criminal law
governing weapons offenses, affrays, and other civil
disturbances on which both sides re lied. Its terms
were taken from militia and international law, not
criminal law, and settled long before 1791.

The Amendment’s two halves, assumed to conflict,
were equivalent formulations of the militia system in
founding-era state constitutions. The terms “keep”
and “bear arms” described public duties, not private
rights, centuries before. George Mason combined
both formulations into a composite militia-and-arms
declaration. New York substituted that declaration

 
for a structural proposal, and Madison adopted it as
a prudent safeguard. None  of this was addressed in
Heller. Nor did Heller address the terms Madison
added—“security” and “infringed,” that strengthened
that safeguard—leaving key text undecided.

Restoring its lega l context, text, and history
resolves the Amendment’s meaning: it declares and
guarantees the States’ right to maintain militias as
security against federal encroachment—a federalism
check identified  by Justice Stevens and widely
recognized in the 20th century but never proved.3

This brief supplies that proof, and it shows why
Heller should not be extended to AR-15-style rifles
absent rebriefing and reconsideration.

ARGUMENT

 Heller’s Entire Premise Rested on
Speculation—And Was Wrong

Heller held the Second Amendment’s “central
component” was an “ancient” right to arms for selfdefense in the 1689 English Bill of Rights—a right
“clearly” individual an d having “nothing to do with”
militia service. 554 U.S. at 592-93, 599, 608. That
premise, which adopted historical claims from Joyce
Malcolm, To Keep and Bear Arms (1994), was doubly
wrong.


3 See 554 U.S. at 667 (Stevens, J., dissenting) (Amendment was
“designed to protect the right of the States to maintain a wellregulated militia”); id. at 638 n.2 (collecting cases).

 
Malcolm acknowledged that English law
recognized no ancient individual right, but rather a
duty “‘from time out of  mind,’” and that the English
declaration expressly “reaffirm[ed]” existing rights.
She nonetheless speculated that its provision—
“Protestants may have arms”—“seems to have” “very
likely” created a new right, though it “seems empty
rhetoric” and is “no longer a right,” having been “so
gently teased from public use that most Britons have
no notion of when or how” it was withdrawn. Malcolm
2, 9, 115, 119-20, 165.

Such conjecture cannot support the weight Heller
gave it. Nor can the conjecture offered by other
historians in McDonald v. Chicago, who, eight to one,
“tell us that Heller misunderstood a key historical
point”: that “have arms” protected a combined right
of Protestants’ to bear arms and of Parliament to arm
them. 561 U.S. 742, 914-16 (2010) (Breyer, J.
dissenting).

That instrument, an assertion of parliamentary
sovereignty containing “‘slight mention’” of private
rights,4 has never been judicially construed. It
catalogued James II’s efforts to “extirpate the
Protestant Religion and the laws and liberties of this
Kingdom,” then reasserted corresponding ancient
rights and liberties. Its first military provision—an
objection to “keeping a Standing Army” without
Parliament’s consent, and declaration that was
“against Law”—restored Parliament’s right over
armies. The next—causing “good subjects, being

4 Stephen Halbrook, That Every Man Be Armed 46 (1984) (citing
rights to petition and bear arms, misreading latter).

 
Protestants, to be disarmed” while “Papists were both
Armed and Imployed contrary to Law,” and
declaration that “Protestants may have Arms for
their Defence suitable to their Conditions and as
allowed by Law”—restored Parliament’s right to
regulate militia. App’x A, 1a-4a

“Armed and [E]mployed” meant armed and “in
service.” E.g., Malcolm 20-21; U.S. Const. art. I, § 8,
cl. 16. Likewise, the remedy—specifying citizens who
could “have Arms” according to “their Conditions and
as allowed by Law”—derived from foundational
militia acts, infra. “For generations citizens had been
required to contribute arms to the militia according to
their condition, that is, their rank and income.”
Malcolm 120.

In context, the provision resolved a war-powers
dispute, asserting Parliament’s rights against the
crown, not a new private right. A draft declaration
similarly stated: “It is necessary to the publick Safety,
that the Subjects which are Protestants, should
provide and keep Arms for the common Defence[.]”
Malcolm 117. Three years later, Parliament rejected,
169-65, a proposal that “any Protestant may keep a
Musquet in his House” notwithstanding contrary
acts, because it would “arm the mob” and was “not
very safe for any government.” Id. at 126-27. Had the
declaration guaranteed a private right, Parliament’s
rejection would be inexplicable.

Without its core pr emise—speculation in place of
legal construction—little remains of Heller.

 Actual Context, Antecedents, and Origins

A. The Second Amendment Must Be
Construed in Its Legal Context

“Context is everything.” Antonin Scalia, A Matter
of Interpretation  37 (1997). “Part of the statute’s
context is the corpus juris of which it forms a part”—
the “‘entire relevant body of the law for the same
purpose’”—“especially” when codified. Antonin Scalia
& Bryan Garner, Reading Law 252–53, 323 (2012).

The basic error in Second Amendment
jurisprudence is failure to identify its legal context.
“Well regulated Militia,” “security of a free State,” and
“keep and bear Arms” were centuries-old terms of
militia law. Cf. CFPB v. Cmty. Fin. Servs. Ass'n of
Am., Ltd ., 601 U.S. 416, 452-53 (2024) (Alito, J.,
dissenting) (explaining when “‘a word is obviously
transplanted from another legal source’” and
elaborated by centuries of legal history, “‘it brings the
old soil with it’”) (citations omitted).

The parties compounded that error by “anchoring”
their interpretations in irrelevant criminal law,
despite contrary evidence and the controlling
alternative body of law. They also exhibited
“availability” bias, relying on later sources to explain
ancient laws. And the evidence, frequently misread,
refuted rather than supported their theories.

The analysis also confused historical research
with legal construction. Justice Scalia suggested that
interpreting ancient text is “sometimes better suited
to the historian.” Antonin Scalia, Originalism: The

Lesser Evil , 57 U. Cin. L. Rev. 849, 856-57 (1989).
Historical research may assist interpretation, but
construction requires identifying the relevant body of
law and legal meaning under rules it is a lawyer’s
“business to know.” Oliver Wendell Holmes, The Path
of the Law, 10 Harv. L. Rev. 457, 469 (1897).

One is the related-statutes canon: an enactment
using terminology found in earlier enactments,
“especially in the very same field, such as securities
or civil-rights law,” ordinarily carries the same
meaning. Different meanings imported from another
domain “should be rejected.” Reading Law , 323. By
disregarding that canon, militia law, and settled legal
usage, and instead importing criminal-law meanings,
Heller misconceived the Amendment from the outset.

Justice Barrett put the point plainly: “To strip a
word from its context is to strip that word of its
meaning.” Biden v. Nebraska , 600 U.S. 477, 511
(2023) (Barrett, J., concurring). Separating the
Amendment’s words from their legal context, Heller
essentially got everything wrong.

B. Antecedents: The Militia System, Not
Criminal Law

The Amendment’s antecedents lie in the
thousand-year militia system, an institution of
universal, compulsory service dating at least to the
Saxon fyrd in the fifth century. Its earliest surviving
enactment is the Assize of Arms of 1181. Michael
Doubler, I Am the Guard 7-8 (2001).

The colonies inherited the institution and enacted
laws “to organize and discipline the colonists in the
citizen-soldier militia system.” James Whisker, Arms
Makers of Colonial America  15–19 (1992). As United
States v. Miller  recognized, “‘the militia system was
based on the principle of the assize of arms,’” whose
elements “‘appear in all the important enactments.’”
307 U.S. 174, 178-82 (1939) (citations omitted).

Its core elements persisted through the centuries:
organization of the citizen body for public defense;
keeping of specified arms in readiness; bearing arms
at muster and in service; and discipline, enforced
through penalties. Id.; Doubler 7-37; Whisker 15-19.
Only the particulars changed: who was enrolled, who
supplied the arms, and where they were kept.
Whisker 15-17.

Miller properly read the Amendment through
militia law: “The signification attributed to the term
Militia appears from the debates in the Convention,
the history and legislation of Colonies and States, and
the writings of approved commentators.” Id. at 179.
Those sources “show plainly enough” that the militia
comprised “all males physically capable of acting in
concert for the common defense,” “‘enrolled for
military discipline,’” and “bearing arms supplied by
themselves and of the kind in common use at the
time.” Id. (citations omitted).

Applying that body of law, the Court unanimously
held: “With obvious purpose to assure the
continuation and render possible the effectiveness of
such forces,” the Amendment’s declaration and
guarantee “must be interpreted and applied with that

  
end in view.” Id. at 178. That directive accords with
the related-statutes canon: enactments “‘relating to
the same subject[] are to be taken together,” as
“having one object in view, and as acting upon one
system.’” Reading Law 252 (citation omitted).

Miller’s directive has never been repudiated.
Heller simply ignored it.

1. Assize of Arms

The Assize of Arms—the principal English
enactment cited in Miller—established the elements
of subsequent Anglo-American militia acts, including
express duties to “keep” and “bear arms” in defense of
the state. Those usages carried into state
constitutions and the Amendment.

The Assize required freemen, according to rank
and means, to “have” specified military arms; to “bear
these arms in [the king’s] service”; and to “keep them
for the service of” the king and realm, on pain of fines
and imprisonment. The Statute of Winchester of 1285
extended the obligation to public peace, night-watch,
and hue-and-cry, and required “every man to have in
his house” arms, “according to” his means—the same
vocabulary used in the 1689 declaration. Queen
Mary’s militia act of 1557 required all freeman to
“have,” “keep,” and “maintain” arms, according to
condition, in every community.  App’x A, 1a-2a.

Later English militia acts supplied other stock
language. The Militia Act of 1757 declared: “Whereas
a well-ordered and well-disciplined Militia is
essentially necessary to the Safety, Peace and

  
Prosperity of this Kingdom.” 30 Geo. 2 c. 25, pmbl.
(G.B.). That common prefatory phrase, with “well
regulated” substituted for “well-ordered” and “free
State” for “Kingdom,” anticipated state militia acts
and the Amendment. App’x A,, 4a, B.1, 5a-6a.

Heller cited none of these foundational statutes.

The Statute of Northampton of 1328—referenced
in Heller and central to Bruen—belongs to another
legal domain. It proscrib ed carrying “dangerous and
unusual weapons” and prescribed who could carry
weapons, and for what purposes, under criminal law.
554 U.S. at 626, 628 (citing 4 Blackstone 148-149
(1769). That authority does not use “well regulated
Militia,” “security of a free State,” or “keep and bear
Arms,” and has little bearing on those terms’
meaning. Cf. United States v. Rahimi , 602 U.S. 680,
738 (2024) (Barrett, J., concurring).

English commentary confirms the distinction.
Blackstone’s pertinent discussion appears in Chapter
13, “Of the Military and Maritime States”—the
chapter Miller cited, 307 U.S. at 179. It explained that
“no man should take up arms, but with a view to
defend his country and its laws,” and that “it is
because he is a citizen, and would wish to continue so,
that he makes himself for a while a soldier.” 1
Blackstone 408–10 (1765). That discussion is not
found in passages Heller cited concerning criminal
self-defense, 554 U.S. at 594 (citing 3 Blackstone 2-4
(1768)), or offenses against the peace, id. at 626, 628
(citing 4 Blackstone 148-49).

  
Heller concluded that Blackstone’s description of
the English declaration “cannot possibly” concern
militia service. 554 U.S. at 594 (citing 1 Blackstone
136, 139-140). But Blackstone described the
declaration as “only declaratory, throughout, of the
old constitutional law.” 4 Blackstone 372.

Heller also misread Samuel Adams, who tied the
“privilege of possessing arms” to militia duty: a
privilege held “in a province where the law requires
them to be equipped with arms” “as the law directs.”
554 U.S. at 594 (citing Shippen, Boston Gazette, Jan.
30, 1769). Adams likewise described Boston’s call for
inhabitants “to provide themselves with arms for
their defence”—a “resolution of this town to keep
arms for its defence”—as the “constitutional right” of

respondents misread. Resp. Br. 19-20, No. 07-290
(citing E.A., Boston Gazette, Feb. 28, 1769). He
emphasized Blackstone’s description of “have arms
for their defence” as being “‘a public allowance, under
due restrictions.’” Id.

Heller similarly misread Granville Sharp’s
reference to “‘arms of defence and peace’” as private
self-defense. 554 U.S. at 594. Sharp instead explained
that English law “had always required the people to
be armed”—with “arms, or instruments of war”—and
“keep them always ready for defense of the kingdom,”
Granville Sharp, Tracts, Concerning the Ancient and
Only True Legal Means of National Defence, by a Free
Militia 10n–19n (3d ed. 1782)). The individual right
Sharp identified was: “each freeman that bears arms”
held “his right of suffrage,” or “share of legislative
influence” to “regulate the service.” Id. at 42.

  

Heller did not address those explanations, the
tract “A General Militia, Acting by a Well-Regulated
Rotation, Is the Only Safe Means of Defending a Free
People,” or Sharp’s repeated references to the “ancient
usage confirmed by statutes,” including militia, wellregulated, have arms, keep arms, and bear arms, id.
at 35, 75-85—terms carried into colonial and state
militia acts. E.g., Whisker 15-16 (quoting statutes).

2. Articles of Confederation

The Articles of Confederation—the Nation’s first
constitution—is another important enactment Heller
did not address. Their provisions were, with less
detail, “copied almost verbatim” into Article I of the
Constitution. Printz v. United States , 521 U.S. 898,
920 n.10 (1997) (Scalia, J.).

The Articles recognized state authority to “keep
up a well regulated and disciplined militia,” “armed
and accoutered,” and required each State “have ready
for use, in public stores” a “proper quantity of arms.”
They also addressed state “security” and protected
legislative rights from “infringement.” Arts. of
Confed., art. III, art. VI, para. 4, art. IX, para. 4.
Together, the provisions supplied the Amendment’s
immediate constitutional setting.

These organic laws must be read together. The
related-statutes canon required it. And “it can never
be supposed,” Madison explained, that when “copied
into this constitution,” “a different meaning ought to
be attached to” terms from the original. Report of

  
1800. Yet no one in Heller construed their provisions
together.

Comparison of the Articles and Constitution
illuminates not only the meaning of the
Amendment’s terms, but the war-powers dispute that
prompted it. Under the Articles, Congress “governed”
and “regulated” regular forces, while the States
“governed” and “regulated” their militias. Art. VI,
para. 4, art. IX, para. 4. The Constitution retained
federal power to “govern” and “regulate” regular
forces, but no longer subject to state control, and
empowered Congress to “provide for organizing,
arming, and disciplining the Militia,” and to
“govern[]” militia when “employed in Service.” Art. I,
§ 8, cl. 14, cl. 16. The latter left the States’ existing
right to govern their militias when not in federal
service implied.

Antifederalists viewed that gap as existential.
They sought “to restore to the state governments their
powers in matters of internal police,” including the
power to “govern the militia.” Federal Farmer (II),
App’x F.1, 23a. Federalist assurances, for example,
that when not in federal service, “Congress has no
power to govern them. The states then have the sole
government of them,” Edmund Pendleton, Va.
Ratification Convention (June 14, 1788)—were
distrusted as merely verbal.

A related gap involved “security.” The Articles
joined the States for “their common defence, the
security of their Liberties, and their mutual and
general welfare.” Articles,  art. III. The Constitution
recited those objects but expressly provided only for

  
“the common Defence and general Welfare,” Const.
pmbl.; art. I, § 8, cl. 1, leaving security of liberty to
implication, broad checks, and the “guarantee to
every State” of republican government. Id., art. IV, §
4; 1 William Crosskey, Politics and the Constitution
374–77, 392–94, 505 (1953).

Antifederalists, fearing Congress’ new
independent army and militia powers could remove
all state authority, questioned what security
remained against the federal guarantor. George
Mason, objecting that the Constitution left “State
Legislatures no Security,” warned Congress might
“disarm, or render useless the Militia” and “govern by
a standing Army,” the bane of liberty. Madison
responded: “I cannot conceive that this Constitution,
by giving the general government the power of
arming the militia, takes it away from the state
governments.” John Marshall likewise argued: “If
Congress neglects our militia, we can arm them
ourselves.” But Patrick Henry rejected assurances
“states have the right of arming” militia, warning
“implication will not save you, when a strong army”
comes. If “a concurrent power” was intended, “where
can be the impolicy to amend” the Constitution? Va.
Ratification Convention (June 14, 16, 1788).).  Cf.
Doubler 64-66.

Heller addressed none of these textual gaps . The
dissents recognized “Article I contained a significant
gap”: that it did not prevent Congress from disarming
the militia. 554 U.S. at 655 (Stevens, J., dissenting).
But they did not address the constitutional text,
particularly that bearing on “regulated” and
“security.”

3. State constitutions
Heller also overlooked the founders’ “better school
of political wisdom in the republican constitutions of
their several States, which many of them had
assisted to frame.” Pollock v. Farmers’ Loan & Trust
Co., 157 U.S. 429, 558 (1895).

State declarations of rights used two formulations
to describe the same militia system, in three clauses
dubbed “Mason Triads.” The Virginia model, drafted
by Mason and followed by Delaware, Maryland, and
New Hampshire, began by describing a “well
regulated militia” as the “safe defence of a free state.”
The Pennsylvania model recognized the people’s
right to “bear arms for defence of themselves and the
state,” or the “common defence” in Massachusetts, as
clarified by John Adams, or simply “the state” in
North Carolina. Both added identical second and
third clauses warning against standing armies and
requiring government by civil authority.  App’x C.1,
C.2, 8a-11a.

Their language “was slightly different, but the
meaning was th e same.” Lawrence Cress, An Armed
Community, 71 J. of Am. Hist. 22, 29 (June, 1984).
Both “fundamentally declared exactly the same
thing.” David Young, The Founders’ View of the Right
to Bear Arms 72 (2007).

The States’ own enactments equated them. States
using the militia model exempted conscientious
objectors from “bearing arms.” Conversely, bear-arms
states like North Carolina and Pennsylvania
introduced corresponding militia acts declaring: “a

   
well regulated militia is absolutely necessary for the
Defending and securing the Liberties of a free State.”
App’x C.3, C.4, 11a-13a.

Heller also misread Pennsylvania’s and Vermont’s
reference to “defence of themselves and the state” as
a “clear” individual right. 554 U.S. at 584-85. That
overlooked thei r companio n exhortation  that every
citizen “is bound” to “yield his personal service when
necessary,” and their conscientious-objectors
exemption from “bearing arms.” App’x C.5.a, 13a-15a.
A person may be exhorted to  perform—and excused
from—a duty, not a right. Both confirm “bear arms”
referred to compulsory militia service. So does the
related-statutes canon. Pennsylvania’s 1755 militia
act authorized citizens willing to “defend themselves
and their Country” (Pennsylvania) when “formed into
regular Bodies for that Purpose” under “suitable and
legal Authority.” Defending “themselves” meant
collective local defense through militia service—as
Samuel Adams explained—not individual selfdefense. App’x C.5.b, 15a.

Heller relied on later wording—“himself and the
state”—to construe use of “themselves and the state”
at founding. 554 U.S. at 584-85, 602-03. The later
language began with the Mississippi Constitution of
1817. Id. at 585 n.8. By then, even this Court had
speculated about the Amendment’s meaning.
Houston v. Moore, 18 U.S. 1, 52-53, 76 (1820) (Story,
J., dissenting).

Heller likewise confused “disarming,” e.g., 554
U.S. at 592-93, over looking that militia statutes
ordered the seizure of arms  Catholics and other

 	 
religious minorities “have or keep in his house.”
App’x D.1, 16a;  Whisker 15-16, 19-20. During
wartime, religious identity shifted to political
allegiance. App’x D.2, 16a-19a. After Shays'
Rebellion, Massachusetts disqualified insurgents
from service, prompting New Hampshire to propose
its singular amendment—a check on selective federal
enrollment to neutralize militia. App’x D.3, 19a. The
fear was Congress’ ability to “disarm, or render
useless the Militia,” as Mason said—not a
generalized power to disarm individuals.

Heller also neglected John Adams, who coined
“keep and bear arms,” and whose Thoughts on
Government (1776) influenced adoption of state
constitutions and accompanying militia laws.
Following the Shays and Articles crises, Adams
published A Defence of the Constitutions of
Government of the United States (1787), that likewise
influenced federal constitutional design and provides
extensive founding-era discussion of the militia
system incompatible with Heller’s account. See infra
at 27.
C. Origins: Walkouts, Non-signers, and
Holdouts

1.  Mason’s militia-and-arms
composite

Mason, a principal non-signer of Constitution,
objected to the absence of a declaration of rights,
including an express protection for state militia. He
said such a declaration could be prepared “in a few


 
hours” with “the aid of the State declarations.” App’x
E.1, 20a-23a.

For Virginia’s ratifying convention, Mason
combined, largely verbatim, the States’ militia and
arms formulations into a composite declaration—each
half expressing the same militia system. Supra Point
II.B.3. Mason took the militia language from
Virginia’s constitution, which he drafted; the arms
language from Massachusetts’ constitution, drafted
by John Adams; and added the remaining elements of
his familiar triad. App’x E.2, 25a-26a.

Mason forwarded the proposal to New York for its
ratifying convention. Id. (editor’s note). His proposed
amendments omitted Virginia’s separate structural
proposal authorizing the States to organize, arm, and
discipline the militia if Congress failed to do so.  Id.
That omission strongly indicates that Mason
regarded his militia-and-arms composite as sufficient
to restore the States’ express authority over the
militia.

2. New York substituted the
composite for a structural proposal

New York’s ratification convention played a
central role in the Amendment’s development.
Standard accounts overlook that New York
transformed a structural militia proposal into
Mason’s militia-and-arms composite.

New York initially considered structural proposals
after Federal Farmer , now identified as Melancton
Smith, urged a guarantee that the Militia “shall

  
always be kept well organized, armed, and
disciplined,” according to past usages. App’x E.1, 24a-
25a. Antifederalists Smith and John Lansing
advanced that approach, as “explanatory” of the
Constitution. Young 150. Federalists by James Duane
proposed a parallel proposal, conditioned on
Congress’ failure to act. App’x E.2, 28a-29a.

The disagreement centered on one phrase:
Federalists regarded “past usages” of the militia as
“indefinite.” Governor Clinton summarized the
common aim: “the object is to keep the Militia well
armed,” and directed that “the Com[mitt]ee will word
it.” The committee replaced the structural proposals
with Mason’s composite, which New York adopted.
App’x E.2, 29-30a. Young 150-51. New York thus
treated the composite as sufficient to restore express
State authority over the militia.

3. State holdouts proposed a
consensus amendment

Most States ratified without proposing a militia
amendment. Of the four States that initially withheld
ratification, Virginia, followed by North Carolina,
proposed Mason’s militia-and-arms composite
together with a structural amendment. App’x F.2,
26a-28a. New York, followed by Rhode Island,
proposed only Mason’s composite, treating a
corresponding structural amendment as unnecessary.
App’x E.2, 29a-30a.

Thus all four holdout States adopted Mason’s
militia-and-arms composite as an express safeguard
of their right to maintain a militia.

  
4. Madison adopted the consensus
amendment

After the Constitutional Convention walkouts and
refusals to sign, Madison transmitted to Jefferson a
summary of state proposals for “further guards to
public liberty & individual rights.” Madison believed
“jealousy of the subordinate Governments” provided
“security” against federal overreach, but
acknowledged the risk of federal “subversion of
liberty” and concluded “it is prudent to guard agst. it.”
App’x E.3, 31a.

By the time Madison drafted the Bill of Rights in
New York City, militia proposals had narrowed to the
single consensus amendment New York had
substituted for structural language and deemed
explanatory. Madison drew not from competing
proposals, as generally assumed, but from the
formulation on which non-signer Mason and all
holdout States had converged.
Madison adopted the consensus amendment in
New York’s form, as well as New York’s broader
ordering of amendments and preface. But he made
two material changes, substituting “security” for
“defence” and adding “shall not be infringed.” Both
terms had settled meanings in federal and state
organic law and concerned state security and
legislative authority. App’x E.3, 31a-32a.
Madison also added: “no person religiously
scrupulous of bearing arms shall be compelled to
render military service in person.” That exemption
makes little sense if the Amendment protected an

  
individual right of self-defense, as the Heller majority
held, or a right to serve, as the dissents supposed.

Thereafter, the House reversed the order of the
Mason composite into its final militia-and-arms form.
The Senate eliminated Madison’s conscience
exemption and reduced “best security” to “security.”
App’x E.4, 32a-33a.
Focused on Madison’s provision that the Senate
rejected, the parties and Heller did not address the
consensus amendment that Madison adopted as the
“guard” against federal “subversion of liberty” he
deemed prudent, or the two terms he added to clarify
it.
5. Consensus amendment satisfied
Antifederalist demands

Mason—whose central objection was the absence
of an explicit concurrent state power over militia—
recorded “much Satisfaction” with the proposed
amendments, including the consensus amendment he
had drafted and Madison had strengthened. App’x
E.5, 33a-34a.

The resulting language closely tracks the States’
right under the Articles to “keep up a well regulated
and disciplined militia, sufficiently armed,” while
echoing the Article’s protection against infringement
of state internal affairs. It completed the Militia
Clauses’ structure by expressly securing the ability of
the States—often termed “the people,” infra Point
IV.C—to maintain an armed militia.

  
Heller acknowledged that ratification debate
centered on “the institution of the state militia,” but
assumed that concern appeared only in the
unadopted structural proposal. 554 U.S. at 603. It did
not recognize that the Amendment addressed the
same concern through a declaratory guarantee:
forbidding infringement of the States’ right to
maintain their militia as security against federal
neglect or abuse. As Justice Stevens later observed,
the Amendment “serves the structural function of
protecting the States from encroachment by an
overreaching Federal Government.” McDonald, 561
U.S. at 897.
 Purpose: Securing States Against the
Federal Guarantor

Heller recognized the “prefatory clause announces
the purpose for which the right was codified”—“A well
regulated Militia, being necessary for the security of
a free State”—but held that the clause “does not limit”
the right, relying on authority concerning detached
preambles. 554 U.S. at 578 & n.3, 599. A prefatory
clause in the same sentence, however, is a “limitation”
that “may not be ignored.” Graham v. John Deere Co.,
383 U.S. 1, 6 (1966). And the House Committee of
Style inverted Mason’s and Madison’s proposed order
to an ablative absolute—a dependent phrase
modifying the rest of the sentence.

Moreover, the “purpose of the text” is a “vital part
of its context,” itself a “primary determinant of
meaning.” Reading Law 33, 167-68. The fact that the
Amendment’s two halves denote the same militia

  
system further supports that the militia clause
explains the arms clause.

Compounding its error, Heller did not construe
“security,” explain Madison’s substitution for
“defence,” or construe “security of a free State” as a
whole. “Every word must be given its due force, and
appropriate meaning.” Holmes v. Jennison , 39 U.S.
540, 570–71 (1840). Each is “affected by other
provisions of the same statute.” Reading Law, 167,
252. Disregarding that canon, Heller missed the
clause’s specific purpose.

The Articles, Constitution, and state constitutions
distinguished ordinary defense from security of public
liberty against usurpation. Madison’s Virginia, for
example, declared that government is “instituted for
the common benefit, protection, and security,” the
latter secured against “maladministration” and
“tyranny.” App’x G, 34a.

Addressing the constitutional gap that left
security of public liberty  implied, supra Point II.B.2.
John Smilie asked: “‘Congress guarantees to each
state a republican form of government.’ Is this a
security for a free government? Can even the shadow
of state governments be continued if Congress please
to take away, or annihilate, the militia?” App’x G, 35a.

The Guarantee Clause resembled a treaty
guarantee of another state’s integrity—an exception
to the non-interference principle that one state may
not infringe another’s internal affairs. But
guarantees “to defend the particular constitution of a
State” often proved “fatal to her liberties and to her

  
very existence.” 2 Robert Phillimore, Commentaries
Upon International Law  71 (London 1855); 1 id. at
441. Smilie rejected the argument that the people’s
ultimate power to abolish the federal government
rendered a lesser check “superfluous.” App’x G, 35a.

The Second Amendment was that check. As
Elbridge Gerry, another non-signer, explained,
without recorded contradiction, it was “intended to
secure the people”—the States—“against the maladministration of the government”—the federal
government. App’x G, 35a-36a. By preserving state
militia as security for public liberty, the Amendment
supplied a reciprocal guarantee against misuse of the
Guarantee Clause and federal military powers.
  Actual Meaning: State Right Not to Be
Infringed

 Heller Rewrote “Well Regulated
Militia” into Unsupported
Abstractions

Heller concluded, in a sentence, that “well
regulated” “implies nothing more than” “discipline
and training.” 554 U.S. at 597. That conclusion
overread its sole founding source, Virginia’s 1776
constitution, and is refuted by Virginia’s 1777 and
1779 “Act[s] for Regulating and Disciplining the
Militia,” whose openings explain both terms: “forming
the citizens of this commonwealth into a militia, and
disciplining the same for defence thereof.” App’x H,
36a-37a. “Form” was similarly used in Pennsylvania’s
1755 militia act, supra, and is the plain meaning of
“regulate” in the constitutional provisions concerning

  
regular forces and militias.  See supra Point II.B.2;
F1.

Further, treating “Regulating and Disciplining”
as synonyms produces “disciplined and disciplined,”
an impermissible “imbecility,” Joseph Story, Rules of
Constitutional Interpretation 190 (1833)—not only
for Virginia’s statutes, but the Articles whose phrase
“well regulated and disciplined militia” governed the
Amendment’s drafting. As Madison warned, terms
copied into the Constitution cannot be given a
different meaning.

Heller similarly recast “militia” as a “citizens’
militia,” citing no authority. 554 U.S. at 595–96. It
acknowledged “militia” means “the same thing” in
the Amendment and Article I’s Militia Clauses, but
reasoned Article’s I’s reference to organizing “the
Militia,” rather than “a Militia,” presupposed an
existing body—one it equated with the demographic
pool of all able-bodied men. Id. at 595-96, 599–600.
That semantic abstraction is negated by Article I
itself, which uses definite articles for institutions not
in existence, including “the supreme Court.” Art. 1, §
8, cl. 9.

The relevant existing institution was the States’
militia. The Constitution itself identifies militia as
“the Militia of the several States,” Art. 2, sec. 2, cl. 1;
its syntax, structure, and drafting history confirm
that meaning, Silveira v. Lockyer , 312 F.3d 1052,
1070-72, 1076-86 (9 th Cir. 2002); and the Articles’
precise phrase “well regulated militia” refers to the
militia of “each State.” Art. VI, para. 4. The related-

   
statutes canon and rule against changing copied
meanings require consistent usage.

Contradicting Heller’s assertion that the

John Adams explained that “the sword and
sovereignty go together,” and described the militia as
the “hand” holding the “public sword”—an institution

ever for the support of the laws.” A Defence 474–75,
487. Hamilton, chair of a post-war congressional
militia committee, likewise explained that “wellregulated militia” means “uniformity in organization

 Heller Overlooked the Public
Context of “Right of the *People”
Another central error is Heller’s assumption that,
because the First and Fourth Amendments use “the
people” to denote individual rights, the Second must
also. But the “same words, placed in different
contexts, sometimes mean different things.” Yates v.
United States, 574 U.S. 528, 537 (2015). Its drafter,
Madison, explained that “the states” and “the people”
take their “true sense” from “different applications of
the term.” Report of 1800.
Context controls. The First and Fourth
Amendments address individual rights. The Second is
framed by terms of militia law, and by “shall not be
infringed,” an international-law term protecting
sovereign rights, infra. In that setting, “the people”
denotes a body politic, whose corresponding “right” is
public.

Founding usage often treated “the people” and
“State” as interchangeable—for example, “the states,
or the people assembled in the state legislatures.”
Federal Farmer  (X), App’x F.1, 24a. English usage
likewise called the House of Commons “the People.”
State legal process was styled, as today, in the name
of the “People” in New York, “Commonwealth” in
Pennsylvania, “State” in North Carolina, or both in
Vermont. Compare People v. Royalton & Woodstock
Tnpk. Co., 11 Vt. 431 (1839) with State v. Nixon , 18
Vt. 70, 75 (1846) (“[T]o designate the sovereign power,

  
we usually say—The State of Vermont;” or “by the
term—The People.”).

States possess powers and rights: powers when
viewed internally, as authority to legislate, tax, and
punish; and rights when viewed externally, authority
exercisable against another sovereign free from
interference. Point IV.E. The Articles protected state
“legislative right” over internal affairs against federal
“infringement,” and reserved to each State every
“power, jurisdiction and right” not delegated. The
Ninth and Tenth Amendments divided that
reservation; the Ninth’s reservation of “rights ...
retained by the people” includes public rights, App’x
B.2, 6a-8a, not merely unenumerated private
liberties.

Recent decisions underscore Heller’s error.
Applying the “specific context,” the Vermont Supreme
Court held that its Constitution’s “right of the people
to bear arms for defence of themselves and the state,”
falls within “the category of rights” “exercised by the
body politic, like “regulating the internal police.”
State v. Misch, 2021 VT 10, ¶¶ 27–29 (2021). See also
Barris v. Stroud Twp. , 310 A.3d 175, 180 n.4 (Pa.
2024) (declining to assume Heller correctly
interpreted Pennsylvania’s identical provision).

In the Second Amendment, “right of the people”
refers to a public right—not merely an unenumerated
retained right, as Federalists argued, but the express
right Antifederalists demanded.

Heller also recast Miller’s description of “arms”—
“ordinary military equipment” “in common use at the
time,” 307 U.S. at 179—as “weapons typically
possessed by law-abiding citizens for lawful
purposes.” 554 U.S. at 625. That abstraction,
assumed to control these cases, appears nowhere in
the Constitution . Miller quoted military
specifications that “show plainly” what “arms”
meant, and empha sized penalties for delinquency to
ensure possession. 307 U.S. at 179-82. See Whisker
17-18 (citing examples). One originalist scholar called
Heller’s reformulation “bizarre,” having “zero
historical support,” and a “test Justice Scalia
invented.” Nelson Lund, The Second Amendment,
Heller, and Originalist Jurisprudence , 56 UCLA L.
Rev. 1343, 1364, 1366-67 (2009).

The only reported decision to cite Miller’s reliance
on the Assize recognized that “the right to keep and
bear arms is meant solely to protect the right of the
states to keep and maintain armed militia,” Hickman
v. Block, 81 F.3d 98, 101-02 & n.8 (9th Cir. 1996). That
conclusion accords with the prior understanding. See
supra n.3. And it follows from the applicable canons,

  
which require enactments to be read in context,
consistently, and as a whole.
 Heller Never Construed “Shall Not
Be Infringed”
Worse still, Heller did not construe the verb on
which the Amendment rests. Instead, it transposed
“infringed” to “abridged,” 554 U.S. at 599, 606—a
substitution not “tolerated” in constitutional
construction. Ogden v. Saunders, 25 U.S. 213, 267-68
(1827). Where terms “cannot, in any appropriate
sense, be said to be synonymous,” treating them as if
they “signify the same thing” would “defeat the
obvious purposes of both.” Houston, 18 U.S. at 64
(Story, J., dissenting).

“Abridge” appears in the First Amendment and
later amendments protecting personal rights.  It
derives from social-contract theory: natural rights,
Hobbes explained, “may by the Civill Law be
abridged.”

“Infringe,” by contrast, is found in three of four
organic laws—the Articles  of Confederation
(providing “the legislative right of any state ... be not
infringed”), Northwest Ordinance (incorporating the
Articles), and the Second Amendment—to protect
sovereign rights.
The term was drawn from the law of nations. The
Peace of Westphalia codified principles of jurisdiction,
territoriality, and non-interference against an
“Infringer” of peace among nations. The Treaty of
Utrecht likewise required that no nation “infringe”

  
the “rights of any other.” Vattel, who often supplied
“the reason for using” terms in the Constitution,
Holmes, 39 U.S. at 570-71, 616-17, explained that
because nations are “free and independent,” each is
entitled to “peaceable enjoyment” of its liberty and no
state may “infringe upon [another’s] perfect rights.” 1
Emer de Vattel, The Law of Nations, prelims. § 15
(1758).
The Federalist invoked the history of the Peace of
Westphalia and Dutch union in explaining federalism
and the States’ “residuary and inviolable
sovereignty” beyond enumerated federal jurisdiction.
Federalist 19, 20, 39; Printz, 521 U.S. at 921 n.11.
Divided sovereignty meant that “mutual rights and
powers” would “infringe occasionally upon each
other.” Smith v. Turner, 48 U.S. 283, 549, 553 (1849)
(Woodbury, J., dissenting). “Infringement” likewise
described encroachment upon public franchises and
patents—“the history of America.” Johnson v.
M’Intosh, 21 U.S. 543, 574, 579-86 (1823).
The distinction between infringed and abridged
appears throughout colonial protests and foundingera legal materials. See App’x H, 37a-53a. Jefferson’s
Summary View of the Rights of British America
(1774), for example, d istinguished public rights—no
legislature may “infringe on the rights and liberties
of another”—from natural rights that law might
“take[] away or abridge[].” App’x H, 40a-41a.

The exception for rights of conscience confirms the
distinction. J efferson explained that religious belief
was “not the object of civil government” and “not
under its jurisdiction”; restraints on belief constituted

  
“an infringement” of divine sovereignty. By contrast,
“all other natural rights[] may be abridged … by the
law.” Thomas Jefferson, Constitutionality of
Residence Bill of 1790.

The First Congress retained that distinction.
Madison’s proposed First Amendment used
“abridged” for civil rights and “infringed” for rights of
conscience. The House altered the civil-rights
language to “infringed”; the Senate restored
“abridging.” By contrast, every version of the Second
Amendment—from Madison’s proposal through the
final text—used “infringed.” App’x H, 32a-33a.

Case law reflects the usage and distinction. E.g.,
New York v. United States , 505 U.S. 144, 177, 181
(1992) (describing federal action “infringing upon the
core of state sovereignty reserved by the Tenth
Amendment” as contrary to federalism’s
“fundamental purpose”); Worcester v. Georgia, 31 U.S.
515, 558-59, 568 (1832) (addressing Articles’
restriction on Congress’ power to “infringe” state
legislative rights and a Georgia statute barring acts
that “abridge the right or privileges of any Indian”).
One Second Amendment case distinguished between
“abridgment personal rights and “infringement” of
political rights.  English v. State,  35 Tex. 473, 477
(1872).

Heller addressed none of this, either. It gave
“infringed” no heading or analysis, although the
Amendment turns on that word.
This Court has since corrected a related
misconception, holding patent infringement concerns

  
a “public right.” Oil States Energy Services, LLC v.
Greene’s Energy Group, LLC , 584 U.S. 325, 334–36
(2018). But Oil States likewise did not consider the
meaning of “infringement” or its use for public rights.

  Heller Should Be Rebriefed And
Reconsidered

A. Heller Has No Binding Effect in These
Cases

That conclusion follows from ordinary principles
of stare decisis. Heller is bounded first by its question
presented: whether handgun restrictions “violate” the
Second Amendment rights of “individuals.” Pet. Br., i
(No. 07-290); 554 U.S. at 573, 635. That question
assumed away the Amendment’s actual text and
right, as did oral argument: “at issue this morning is
the scope and nature of the individual right.” Tr. 3
(Mar. 18, 2008).

Second, Heller binds only as to questions decided,
not terms left unconstrued or premises assumed.
Pollock, 157 U.S. at 574-76. Other courts have
recognized that a decision overlooking pivotal text
“cannot stand” and has “nothing to contribute.” E.g.,
Fluor Corp. v. Superior Court, 61 Cal. 4th 1175, 1182
(2015); State v. Sandoval , 342 Ore. 506, 512-13
(2007). Because Heller did not construe key
constitutional terms—“security” and “infringed”—or
construe the Amendment as a whole, it cannot be
extended to these cases.

   
B. Heller’s Consequences Confirm the
Need for Reconsideration

Heller’s consequences are starkly evident. “Our
Nation is gripped by a level of deadly gun violence our
founders never could have conceived.” Barris, 310
A.3d at 215 (joining “ever-growing chorus” urging the
Court “to reconsider its path entirely”).

By constitutionalizing broad firearms possession,
Heller magnifies the predictable consequences of
anger, passion, intoxication, and impaired impulse
control. See 554 U.S. at 694 (Breyer, J., dissenting).
Its costs are measured not only in lives but are
widespread.

Justice Scalia had urged overruling a “judgeinvented doctrine” and “mess I helped make” once its
error became “glaringly obvious.” Michigan v. Bay
Mills Indian Cmty., 572 U.S. 782, 814 (2014) (Scalia,
J., dissenting). The same willingness to reconsider is
warranted here.

CONCLUSION

The Court should direct briefing on the question
Justice Barrett identified, reconsider Heller, and
decide the Second Amendment according to its legal
context, text, and meaning.
